passages.t: ‘I envied the arrogant’: a faithful man nearly slips
passages.happening:
Psalm 73 opens Book Three of the Psalms. The heading reads, “A Psalm of Asaph” (verse 1). Asaph's name stands over Psalm 50 and over every psalm from 73 to 83.

The psalm starts with the answer and then tells how hard it was to reach. “Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart” (verse 1). Then at once: “But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped” (verse 2).

What tripped him was envy. “For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (verse 3). He paints them in detail. They are healthy and well fed (verse 4). They seem free of the troubles other people carry (verse 5). “Therefore pride is their necklace; a garment of violence covers them” (verse 6). They mock God: “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” (verse 11).

Then comes the bitter part. “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands” (verse 13). “For I am afflicted all day long and punished every morning” (verse 14). He has done what was right, and it seems to have earned him nothing.
passages.hearers:
Asaph, the book page says, led the temple singers in David's day (1 Chronicles 16:7), and his family went on singing for centuries. So a psalm of Asaph may come from Asaph himself or from a singer of his line. The man who speaks here may have stood in the temple choir. That makes his doubt sharper. It is a worship leader who nearly lost his faith.

His trouble grows out of what Israel had been taught. Psalm 1 says the righteous flourish like a tree and the wicked blow away like chaff. Proverbs says much the same. Psalm 37 told its hearers not to envy evildoers, because they will soon wither. This man knows all that. His problem is that his eyes tell him something else.

Notice the small word ‘Surely’. In Hebrew it is one short word, and it comes three times (verses 1, 13 and 18). In verse 1 it states the faith. In verse 13 it states the doubt: ‘surely in vain’. In verse 18 it states what he learns. The whole psalm swings between those three ‘surely’s.

In a land where many went hungry, a well-fed body (verse 4) was a mark of wealth. Washing the hands (verse 13) was a way of saying ‘I am innocent’ (Psalm 26:6).
passages.later:
This question runs all through the Bible. Job asks, “Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” (Job 21:7). Jeremiah says to God, “Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” (Jeremiah 12:1). Neither man is scolded for asking. God answers Job, and the book of Job says Job spoke rightly of God, not his comforters (Job 42:7).

Jesus told of a rich man who lived in comfort while a poor man named Lazarus lay at his gate (Luke 16:19-31). In the story, death turned their places around. Jesus also said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8). Psalm 73 begins with the pure in heart, and ends with a man who has seen God.
passages.hard:
Is it wrong to feel what this man felt? The psalm does not hide it, and it does not pretend he was calm. He says his feet almost slipped. He says his faith seemed pointless. And God kept his words in Scripture, and set them at the head of a whole book of the Psalms.

If you have doubts like these, this psalm does not scold you. It shows you a believer who had them too, who said them out loud to God, and who was not thrown out for saying them. Doubt spoken to God is still a kind of prayer. The man in Psalm 73 did not find his answer by pretending. He found it by bringing his question into God's house.

There is one thing he chose not to do, and verse 15 says what it was. The next passage takes that up.
passages.asks:
Be honest about where envy has caught you. It may be a neighbour's money, a colleague's ease, or someone whose life seems to work while yours does not. Name it, as this psalm does.

Then notice that he did not stop at the envy. He kept talking to God. If your faith feels like it is slipping, you do not need to hide that from God. Tell him, in your own words or in these.

passages.happening:
Here the psalm turns. First he says what held him back from spreading his doubt. “If I had said, ‘I will speak this way,’ then I would have betrayed Your children” (verse 15). He did not want his bitterness to knock others off their feet.

But keeping quiet did not solve it. “When I tried to understand all this, it was troublesome in my sight” (verse 16). Thinking harder only made it heavier.

Then comes the turning point of the whole psalm: “until I entered God's sanctuary; then I discerned their end” (verse 17). He saw where the road of the wicked was going. “Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin” (verse 18). “How suddenly they are laid waste, completely swept away by terrors” (verse 19). Their glory is like a dream. When a person wakes, the dream is gone (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The sanctuary was the temple in Jerusalem, the place of sacrifice, prayer and the worship of God's people. The psalm does not say what happened to him there. It may have been the words of Scripture read aloud. It may have been the praise of the people. It may simply have been time in God's presence. The psalm leaves it open, and so do these notes.

What changed was not the facts. The wicked were still rich when he walked out. What changed was how far he could see. In the temple he saw ‘their end’, the place where their road comes out. He had been looking at a snapshot. Now he saw the whole film.

Verse 15 shows a wise kind of care. He does not deny his doubt. He brings it to God. But he is slow to make it the song he teaches the children of God before he has finished thinking it through.
passages.later:
Jesus told of a rich farmer who planned bigger barns and said to himself that he could take life easy. God said to him, “You fool! This very night your life will be required of you” (Luke 12:20). Jesus said, “one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15).

Paul compares what is seen with what lasts. “For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).
passages.asks:
Where do you take your hardest questions? This man found his answer when he came into the presence of God with God's people. You may find that worship, Scripture and prayer with others let you see further than you can alone.

And think about verse 15. Doubts are not shameful, and you may speak them to God and to people you trust. But be careful what you hand on to those who are young in faith before you have wrestled it through.

passages.t: ‘Whom have I in heaven but You?’
passages.happening:
Now he looks back on himself. “When my heart was grieved and I was pierced within, I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You” (verses 21 to 22). He is not proud of how he thought.

Then the most surprising word in the psalm: ‘Yet’. “Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand” (verse 23). Even while he was a ‘brute beast’, God had not let go of him. “You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory” (verse 24).

Then he finds what he really wants. “Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You” (verse 25). “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (verse 26).

The psalm ends where it began, with what is good. “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
‘My portion’ (verse 26) would mean a great deal to a temple singer. When the land of Israel was shared out, the priests and Levites received none. God said to Aaron, “I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites” (Numbers 18:20). A Levite owned no farm. God himself was his share.

Look at what the man does not say. He does not say, ‘Now I am rich too.’ He does not say his troubles have ended. He says that God is enough, even if body and heart give out.

‘Later receive me in glory’ (verse 24) is one of the lines in the Psalms that reach past death. The word for ‘receive’ is the word used when God took Enoch (Genesis 5:24). Some readers think the psalmist meant only that God would bring him back to honour in this life. Others think he glimpsed a hope beyond the grave. The book page sets out these readings in its part on Sheol.
passages.later:
Jesus said of his sheep, “No one can snatch them out of My hand” (John 10:28). Psalm 73 found God holding the right hand of a man who felt like a beast.

Paul wrote, “neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38-39). And he wrote, “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).
passages.asks:
Psalm 73 does not end by giving the doubter what the wicked had. It ends by giving him God. Ask yourself what you would want if you could have only one thing. The man in this psalm, after all his envy, answered: God himself.

If you are in the middle of doubt, hold on to verse 23. You may feel senseless before God, and God may still be holding your hand. Pray verse 25 slowly, and ask him to make it true of you.
